Grief & Loss: Carrying What Cannot Be Fixed

Grief is not a staircase you climb. It is weather you learn to live inside.

Overview

Grief is not only about death. It follows divorce, diagnosis, estrangement, miscarriage, and the loss of a future you had assumed. Any of those can produce the full physical weight of mourning.

The five-stage model was originally observed in dying patients, not the bereaved, and was never intended as a checklist. Grief does not progress tidily, and revisiting an earlier feeling is not regression.

Oscillation, not stages

Current models describe grief as moving back and forth between confronting the loss and attending to ongoing life. Both are necessary. A morning of laughter does not undo mourning, and a wave of sorrow two years on is not a relapse.

Grief also lives in the body: appetite changes, disrupted sleep, chest heaviness, and a real hit to concentration and immune function. This is why practical care — food, water, sleep — is legitimate grief work.

Signs & Patterns to Notice

These are common patterns and bodily stress responses rather than a formal diagnosis:

  • [Mind] Waves rather than a slope: Intensity arrives suddenly, often triggered by something small and ordinary.
  • [Body] Physical heaviness: Chest pressure, aching limbs, and exhaustion that sleep does not touch.
  • [Behavior] Searching behaviour: Scanning crowds, rereading messages, keeping a phone number active.
  • [Mind] Guilt and rehearsal: Replaying what might have been said or done differently.

What People Believe vs. What Evidence Shows

Myth: “Grief lasts about a year.”

Fact: There is no schedule. Acute grief often softens over months, but adaptation continues for years and anniversaries stay tender.

Myth: “Staying busy is the healthiest approach.”

Fact: Distraction has a place, but grief that is never approached tends to surface as physical symptoms or sudden collapse.

Myth: “Moving forward means letting go.”

Fact: Most people keep a continuing bond with the person they lost. Integration, not erasure, is the goal.

Practical Coping Strategies

Continuing-bond letters

Keeps the relationship present in a form you control.

  1. Write to them, not about them — present tense.
  2. Include ordinary news, not only sorrow.
  3. Stop when it becomes heavy; there is no requirement to finish.

Anniversary planning

Removes the dread of being ambushed by a date.

  1. Mark the date and decide in advance who you want nearby.
  2. Choose one small ritual — a walk, a meal they loved, a candle.
  3. Give yourself explicit permission to cancel everything else.

Baseline care card

Reduces daily decisions to a short, achievable list.

  1. Write four items: water, one meal, outside air, one message answered.
  2. Keep it visible in the kitchen.
  3. Treat a partly ticked card as a completed day.

How to Support Someone Nearby

Helpful phrases to say:

  • ““I remember when she used to do this — I still think about it.””
  • ““I have no words that help, but I am not going anywhere.””
  • ““I am coming over Saturday to do the laundry, not to talk.””

Phrases to avoid:

  • ““They are in a better place now.””
  • ““Everything happens for a reason.””
  • ““At least you had many years together.””

Common Questions

When is grief a clinical concern?

If after twelve months there is persistent, intense yearning with an inability to function, prolonged grief disorder may apply and specific treatment helps.

Should children attend a funeral?

Usually yes, if they want to and are prepared for what they will see. Exclusion tends to increase confusion rather than reduce distress.

Why do I feel relief alongside sorrow?

Relief is extremely common, especially after long illness or a difficult relationship. It coexists with love rather than contradicting it.
